es.summary: Inflamación de la mucosa del estómago que puede ser aguda o crónica y suele estar provocada por irritantes, alcohol, H. pylori o estrés.
key_points: Puede ser aguda (irritantes) o crónica (H. pylori, autoinmune).
Síntomas típicos: dolor epigástrico, náuseas, vómitos y, a veces, hematoquecia.
Complicación principal: úlcera péptica y sangrado gastrointestinal.
Tratamiento de primera línea: antiácidos, inhibidores de la bomba de protones y erradicación de H. pylori.

pathophysiology: Los irritantes disminuyen la producción de prostaglandina E2, reduciendo la secreción de moco y bicarbonato.
La pérdida de la barrera mucosa permite que el ácido clorhídrico dañe la epitelia gástrica.
En la gastritis crónica, H. pylori produce inflamación sostenida y daño tisular.
El daño prolongado puede generar erosiones que evolucionan a úlcera péptica.
risk_factors: Consumo excesivo de alcohol y tabaco.
Estrés severo, quemaduras o sepsis prolongada.
signs_symptoms: Dolor epigástrico tipo ardor, a menudo 1‑3 h después de comer.
Náuseas y/o vómitos, a veces con sangre (hematemesis).
Hematoquecia o melena si hay sangrado activo.
Pérdida de apetito y pérdida de peso no intencional.
diagnostics: Endoscopia digestiva alta: mucosa eritematosa, erosiones o úlceras.
Test de aliento o antígeno en heces para H. pylori.
Hemograma: hemoglobina <12 g/dL sugiere sangrado crónico.
Pruebas de sangre oculta en heces si hay melena.
treatment: Antiácidos (hidróxido de aluminio‑magnesio) para alivio rápido.
Inhibidores de la bomba de protones (omeprazol, pantoprazol).
Erradicación de H. pylori: amoxicilina + claritromicina + inhibidor de bomba de protones por 14 días.
Suspender AINEs y evitar alcohol y tabaco.
complications: Úlcera péptica con riesgo de perforación.
Anemia ferropénica por pérdida de sangre.
Estreñimiento o diarrea por uso prolongado de antiácidos.
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor usando escala numérica; registrar localización y factores de alivio.
Monitorear signos vitales, especialmente presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca por posible sangrado.
Observar heces y vómitos para detectar sangre (color rojo brillante o melena).
Administrar medicamentos según orden, verificando tiempo respecto a alimentos.
Mantener NPO o dieta blanda según indicación; posicionar semi‑Fowler para reducir reflujo.
patient_teaching: Tomar antiácidos o inhibidores de bomba de protones según horario, sin omitir dosis.
Evitar AINEs, alcohol, café fuerte y comidas muy grasosas.
Completar el esquema antibiótico si se diagnostica H. pylori.
Reportar cualquier sangrado rectal, vómito con sangre o dolor que empeore.

outcomes: Control del dolor: escala ≤ 3/10 en 48 h
Mejora del confort: paciente reporta alivio del dolor

interventions.action: Evaluar dolor con escala numérica cada 2 h
interventions.rationale: Permite medir la intensidad y la respuesta al tratamiento

interventions.action: Administrar antiácidos o inhibidores de bomba de protones según prescripción
interventions.rationale: Reduce la acidez y alivia la irritación mucosa

interventions.action: Ofrecer posición semi‑Fowler y evitar presión abdominal
interventions.rationale: Disminuye el reflujo y el dolor

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre evitar irritantes (AINEs, alcohol)
Registrar respuesta al analgésico y notificar al médico si el dolor persiste > 5/10

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos
outcomes: Mantener hidratación adecuada: ingesta oral ≥ 1500 mL/día
Peso estable: variación < 0,5 kg en 24 h

interventions.action: Monitorear ingesta y salida de líquidos cada turno
Evaluar signos de deshidratación (turgor, mucosas secas, taquicardia)
interventions.rationale: Identifica déficit de volumen antes de que sea crítico

interventions.action: Administrar soluciones intravenosas según orden si hay pérdida significativa
Ofrecer pequeñas tomas frecuentes de líquidos claros
interventions.rationale: Facilita la tolerancia y reduce el riesgo de vómitos

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de reponer líquidos y reconocer signos de deshidratación

en.summary: Inflammation of the stomach mucosa that can be acute or chronic and is usually caused by irritants, alcohol, H. pylori or stress.
key_points: Can be acute (irritants) or chronic (H. pylori, autoimmune).
Typical symptoms: epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting and sometimes hematochezia.
Main complication: peptic ulcer and gastrointestinal bleeding.
First‑line treatment: antacids, proton pump inhibitors and H. pylori eradication.

pathophysiology: Irritants decrease prostaglandin E2 production, reducing mucus and bicarbonate secretion.
Loss of the mucosal barrier allows hydrochloric acid to damage gastric epithelium.
In chronic gastritis, H. pylori causes sustained inflammation and tissue damage.
Prolonged damage can produce erosions that evolve into peptic ulcer.
risk_factors: Severe stress, burns or prolonged sepsis.
signs_symptoms: Burning epigastric pain, often 1‑3 h after eating.
Nausea and/or vomiting, sometimes with blood (hematemesis).
Hematochezia or melena if active bleeding.
Loss of appetite and unintended weight loss.
diagnostics: Upper endoscopy: erythematous mucosa, erosions or ulcers.
Breath test or stool antigen for H. pylori.
CBC: hemoglobin <12 g/dL suggests chronic bleeding.
Fecal occult blood test if melena present.
treatment: H. pylori eradication: amoxicillin + clarithromycin + proton pump inhibitor for 14 days.
Discontinue NSAIDs and avoid alcohol and tobacco.
complications: Peptic ulcer with risk of perforation.
Iron deficiency anemia from blood loss.
Constipation or diarrhea from prolonged antacid use.
nursing_care: Assess pain using numeric scale; record location and relief factors.
Monitor vital signs, especially blood pressure and heart rate for possible bleeding.
Observe stool and vomitus for blood (bright red or melena).
Administer medications per order, checking timing relative to meals.
Maintain NPO or soft diet as indicated; position semi‑Fowler to reduce reflux.
patient_teaching: Take antacids or proton pump inhibitors as scheduled, do not miss doses.
Avoid NSAIDs, alcohol, strong coffee and very fatty meals.
Complete the antibiotic regimen if H. pylori is diagnosed.
Report any rectal bleeding, vomiting with blood or worsening pain.

outcomes: Pain control: numeric scale ≤ 3/10 within 48 h
Improved comfort: patient reports pain relief

interventions.action: Assess pain with numeric scale every 2 h
interventions.rationale: Allows measurement of intensity and response to treatment

interventions.action: Administer antacids or proton pump inhibitors as prescribed
interventions.rationale: Reduces acidity and relieves mucosal irritation

interventions.action: Offer semi‑Fowler position and avoid abdominal pressure
Educate patient on avoiding irritants (NSAIDs, alcohol)
Document analgesic response and notify physician if pain persists > 5/10

outcomes: Maintain adequate hydration: oral intake ≥ 1500 mL/day
Stable weight: change < 0.5 kg in 24 h

interventions.action: Monitor fluid intake and output each shift
Assess signs of dehydration (turgor, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia)
interventions.rationale: Identifies volume deficit before it becomes critical

interventions.action: Administer IV fluids per order if significant loss
Offer small frequent clear fluid sips
interventions.rationale: Facilitates tolerance and reduces vomiting risk

interventions.action: Educate patient on importance of fluid replacement and recognizing dehydration signs

summary.0.quote: Acute gastritis is usually caused by an irritant, such as aspirin or NSAID use, heavy alcohol use, smoking, and certain infections.

summary.1.quote: Chronic gastritis most commonly is caused by Helicobacter pylori infection ( Figure 19.12 ) but can also be caused by autoimmune disease, Crohn’s disease , gastric surgery, and other infections, such as HIV.

key_points.0.quote: Chronic gastritis most commonly is caused by Helicobacter pylori infection ( Figure 19.12 ) but can also be caused by autoimmune disease, Crohn’s disease , gastric surgery, and other infections, such as HIV.

key_points.2.quote: There is an increased risk for complications, including gastric cancer , peptic ulcers, and gastric bleeding or perforation, when gastritis is untreated (Azer et al., 2023).

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Gastric mucosal cells counteract the HCl acid by secreting prostaglandin E 2 , a strong, lipid-rich molecule that stimulates gastric mucus and pancreatic bicarbonate.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: However, the protective structure of the mucosal membrane may become eroded when exposed to excessive HCl acid and pepsin, especially if these substances permeate the epithelium.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Chronic gastritis most commonly is caused by Helicobacter pylori infection ( Figure 19.12 ) but can also be caused by autoimmune disease, Crohn’s disease , gastric surgery, and other infections, such as HIV.

sections.signs_symptoms.1.quote: Other symptoms include heartburn, dyspepsia, chest discomfort, hematemesis (vomiting of blood), melena (black tarry stools), fatigue, and dyspnea

sections.signs_symptoms.3.quote: Subjective data for a patient with gastritis can include the patient’s report of presence of gastric pain, belching or hiccups, nausea or vomiting, blood in vomit or stool, or loss of appetite.

sections.complications.0.quote: There is an increased risk for complications, including gastric cancer , peptic ulcers, and gastric bleeding or perforation, when gastritis is untreated (Azer et al., 2023).

sections.complications.2.quote: Bloodwork will check for the presence of H. pylori infection and will also check for iron deficiency anemia that can be caused by blood loss in the GI tract.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: Monitor the patient’s stool for the presence of blood in the stool; bloody stool may present as a fresh, bright red color (frank) or dark and tarry.

sections.patient_teaching.3.quote: You should see a doctor if you have any of the following: Blood when you have a bowel movement Severe abdominal pain Heartburn not relieved by antacids Unintended weight loss Ongoing vomiting or diarrhea
